questions.text:
Sulfur forms a range of different fluoride-containing ions and molecules.

Complete the table below, showing the Lewis structure and name of shape for SF₃⁻ and SBrF₅.
questions.expectedAnswer: SF₃⁻: Lewis structure shows S central atom with 3 bonding pairs to F and 1 lone pair.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Two correct entries. One mark per correct Lewis structure and one mark per correct shape name.

questions.text:
The Lewis structure and shape for sulfur tetrafluoride, SF₄, are shown below.

[Diagram shows SF₄ with seesaw shape]

Identify and explain the polarity of SF₄.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies SF₄ as polar and recognises the influence of electronegativity. Merit: Explains the polarity of SF₄ in terms of bond polarity and the asymmetric arrangement of dipoles.

questions.text: Justify why the F–S–F bond angles in SF₄ are different to the F–S–F bond angles in SBrF₅.
questions.expectedAnswer: SF₄ has five areas of electron density around S (4 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair) based on...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: States SF₄ has F–S–F bond angles of 90° and 120°. Merit: Identifies different electron geometries lead to different bond angles. Excellence: Justifies the difference linking to electron pair arrangement and lone pair repulsion in each geometry.

questions.text:
Finely powdered sulfur, S(s), readily reacts with fluorine gas, F₂(g), in an exothermic reaction to produce sulfur hexafluoride, SF₆(g). The equation for the reaction is:

S(s) + 3F₂(g) → SF₆(g)

Justify, in terms of the entropy changes of the system and surroundings, why the reaction is spontaneous.
questions.expectedAnswer: System entropy decreases: 3 highly randomised gas molecules and one solid produce only one gas...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises entropy increases when there is an increase in disorder / dispersal of matter. Merit: Explains entropy change for the system OR surroundings. Excellence: Justifies the spontaneous nature of the reaction in terms of entropy changes in the system and surroundings.

questions.text:
Complete the table below, showing the electron configuration (use s, p, d notations) for:

Cl
Cu
Fe³⁺

Iron, Fe, can form two different ions, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺. Their ionic radii are given below:

Fe²⁺: 92 pm
Fe³⁺: 79 pm

Explain why the radius of the Fe²⁺ ion is larger than the radius of the Fe³⁺ ion.
questions.expectedAnswer: Both ions have the same nuclear charge (26 protons), but Fe²⁺ has more electrons (24) than Fe³⁺...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies same nuclear charge but different numbers of electrons. Merit: Explains that Fe²⁺ has more electrons with the same number of protons, so there is a greater electron-electron repulsion or less effective nuclear charge per electron, leading to a larger radius.

questions.text:
Identify all the types of attractive forces between particles of the following substances in their liquid state.

Hydrogen bromide, HBr(l) — ΔvapH° = 17.3 kJ mol⁻¹
Hydrogen fluoride, HF(l) — ΔvapH° = 25.2 kJ mol⁻¹
Bromine, Br₂(l) — ΔvapH° = 29.6 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.expectedAnswer: HBr: Permanent dipole–dipole (PD–PD) attractions, temporary dipole (TD–TD / London dispersion)...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correctly identifies attractive forces for at least two substances.

questions.text: Explain why the ΔvapH° of HF is higher than that of HBr.
questions.expectedAnswer: HF has hydrogen bonding (due to large electronegativity difference between H and F),
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises hydrogen bonding is stronger. Merit: Explains differences in molarity/electronegativity leading to differences in strength of attractive forces.

questions.text: Justify why Br₂ has the highest ΔvapH° of the three substances.
questions.expectedAnswer: Despite Br₂ having only temporary dipole forces (no permanent dipoles or hydrogen bonding), it...
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises that a larger electron cloud / larger molar mass gives stronger temporary dipole forces. Merit: Explains that Br₂'s large size produces strong temporary dipole forces despite lacking hydrogen bonding. Excellence: Fully justifies by comparing all three substances' attractive force strengths.

questions.text:
Nitric acid, HNO₃, is manufactured from ammonia, NH₃. The equation for one of the reactions in the process is:

4NH₃(g) + 5O₂(g) → 4NO(g) + 6H₂O(l)   ΔᵣH° ≈ −1172 kJ mol⁻¹

Write the balanced equation to represent the standard enthalpy of formation of ammonia in the table below.

[Table shows: NH₃(g) — equation blank — ΔfH° blank; NO(g) — ½N₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → NO(g) — +90.3; H₂O(l) — H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l) — −286]
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct enthalpy of formation equation for NH₃.

questions.text: Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation for ammonia, ΔfH°(NH₃(g)), using the data given in part (i).
questions.expectedAnswer: Using ΔᵣH° = Σ ΔfH°(products) − Σ ΔfH°(reactants): −1172 = [4(90.3) + 6(−286)] − [4(ΔfH° NH₃) + 0].
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct process with one error. Merit: Correct process. Excellence: Correct answer, including unit and 2–4 significant figures.

questions.text:
Dinitrogen tetroxide, N₂O₄, was reacted with methylhydrazine, CH₃NHNH₂. The equation for the reaction is:

4CH₃NHNH₂(l) + 5N₂O₄(l) → 4CO₂(g) + 12H₂O(g) + 9N₂(g)

Calculate the standard enthalpy change of this reaction, using the following data.

C(s) + 3H₂(g) + N₂(g) → CH₃NHNH₂(l)   ΔfH° = +54.1 kJ mol⁻¹
C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)   ΔfH° = −394 kJ mol⁻¹
N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) → N₂O₄(l)   ΔfH° = −20.0 kJ mol⁻¹
H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l)   ΔfH° = −286 kJ mol⁻¹
H₂O(l) → H₂O(g)   ΔvapH° = +40.7 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correctly manipulates one equation/enthalpy change. Merit: Correct process with one error. Excellence: Correct answer with correct unit, sign, and significant figures (2–4).

questions.text: Explain the effect on the standard enthalpy change calculated in part (c)(i) if the water was produced as a liquid.
questions.expectedAnswer: The enthalpy change would be more exothermic / more negative
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises energy is released when gas changes to liquid. Merit: Explains that energy is released as intermolecular forces form between water molecules when changing state from gas to liquid.

questions.text: Justify, using your knowledge of periodic trends, why magnesium, Mg, has a greater first ionisation energy than strontium, Sr.
questions.expectedAnswer: Mg has a greater first ionisation energy than Sr
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises distance/shielding has an effect. Merit: Explains the trend in terms of distance, shielding, and effective nuclear charge. Excellence: Explains the trends in atomic radii across a period linking distance, repulsion, shielding, and nuclear charge.

questions.text:
The atomic radii of five elements from Period 3 are shown in the table below.

Na: 0.191 nm, Mg: 0.160 nm, Al: 0.130 nm, Si: 0.118 nm, P: 0.110 nm

Explain the trend in atomic radius shown in the table.
questions.expectedAnswer: Atomic radius decreases across Period 3 from Na to P.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Recognises that nuclear charge affects atomic radius. Merit: Explains the trend linking nuclear charge and same energy level. Excellence: Explains the trend in atomic radii across a period, including distance, repulsion/shielding, and nuclear charge/attraction.

questions.text:
When solid calcium chloride, CaCl₂(s), dissolves in water, the temperature increases from 20.4 °C to 23.2 °C.

CaCl₂(s) → Ca²⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq)   ΔH = −81.3 kJ mol⁻¹

Calculate the mass of CaCl₂(s) that must dissolve to cause this temperature increase.
Assume the specific heat capacity of the calcium chloride solution is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹.
Assume the mass of the calcium chloride solution is 68.0 g.
M(CaCl₂) = 111 g mol⁻¹
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Calculates heat energy released when CaCl₂ dissolves. Merit: Correct process to determine mass with minor error. Excellence: Calculates mass of CaCl₂, including unit and 2–4 significant figures.
